journal_name: IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems for Video Technology

abstracts.abstract: Current video compression standards predominantly rely on block-based prediction and discrete cosine transform, which have approached their theoretical capacity limits. This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework for video representation based on graph signal processing, fundamentally transforming how video content is analyzed and compressed. We model video sequences as signals on weighted graphs, where spatial-temporal correlations are naturally captured through graph topology. The proposed graph Fourier transform provides a mathematically principled alternative to conventional block-based transforms, enabling content-adaptive representation without fixed grid constraints. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that graph-based representation achieves superior approximation of video signals under sparsity-promoting optimization. Experimental results on standard benchmarks validate that the proposed framework achieves 30-40% bitrate reduction compared to HEVC at equivalent perceptual quality. Furthermore, we establish theoretical bounds on compression efficiency gains based on graph signal smoothness, providing insights into scenarios where content-adaptive coding yields maximum benefit. This work establishes a new theoretical paradigm that challenges the dominance of block-based video coding, opening promising research directions for content-aware video compression.

End-to-end learned video compression has emerged as a promising alternative to traditional hybrid coding frameworks, yet existing approaches suffer from limited temporal modeling capability. Current neural video codecs typically employ sequential frame prediction, which fails to effectively exploit bidirectional temporal dependencies across video sequences. This paper presents a comprehensive theoretical analysis of temporal modeling mechanisms in learned video compression and proposes an enhanced framework that integrates bidirectional temporal prediction with flow-based motion compensation. We theoretically analyze the information-theoretic foundations of predictive coding and derive optimal balance between motion information and residual encoding. The proposed dual-path temporal modeling enables more efficient exploitation of inter-frame redundancies, particularly in sequences with complex motion patterns. Experimental evaluations on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art learned compression approaches by 15-25% in BD-rate reduction while maintaining comparable computational complexity. Objective quality metrics and subjective user studies confirm improved visual quality, especially at low bitrate scenarios. This work provides valuable theoretical insights for designing more effective temporal models in neural video codecs.

The proliferation of ultra-high-definition video applications has created unprecedented challenges for video processing infrastructure, requiring fundamental reimagining of system architectures. This paper presents a programmable video processing pipeline that departs from traditional monolithic designs, introducing a modular edge-cloud collaborative architecture for next-generation video technology. The proposed system incorporates intelligent function decomposition with adaptive task offloading based on real-time performance profiling and quality-of-service requirements. We design novel programmable data planes that enable dynamic adjustment of processing paths without system interruption, supporting heterogeneous video workloads from live streaming to interactive applications. The architecture features hierarchical caching with predictive pre-fetching driven by viewing pattern analysis, significantly reducing content delivery latency. Implementation on commodity hardware platforms demonstrates 45% latency reduction and 38% bandwidth savings for 4K video analysis tasks compared to conventional cloud-centric approaches. The system has been deployed across geographically distributed edge nodes, validating scalability and robustness under real-world conditions. This work represents a paradigm shift from centralized to distributed programmable video processing, addressing critical challenges in modern video technology infrastructure.

Video surveillance systems face increasing demands for real-time intelligent analysis across massive camera networks, yet edge devices at deployment sites have limited computational resources. This paper presents a heterogeneous computing platform for scalable video analytics that significantly improves processing throughput through intelligent resource management. The proposed architecture integrates task scheduling with dynamic workload balancing across heterogeneous hardware accelerators, including CPUs, neural processing units, and edge GPUs. We introduce novel model partitioning techniques that optimally distribute deep neural network inference across available computational resources based on real-time scene complexity analysis. The system incorporates adaptive batching strategies that dynamically adjust processing granularity according to video content characteristics and processing urgency. Extensive evaluations across diverse surveillance scenarios demonstrate 3.2x improvement in system throughput compared to existing approaches, with graceful degradation under overload conditions. The platform maintains end-to-end latency below 100ms for real-time video analysis applications while achieving significant energy efficiency improvements. Practical deployment in urban surveillance networks validates the system's effectiveness in real-world environments. This work provides a practical solution for scalable intelligent video surveillance.
